passage:
At the cyber café in Satara, with the fan clicking overhead, Ojas opened the job pages of three companies he wanted: two logistics firms in Pune and a farm-tech startup. He read each posting slowly and copied the repeating phrases into his notebook: 'cleaning messy data', 'dashboards', 'deployed to the cloud'.
'Look at this,' he said to Sangeeta, his cousin, who ran the café counter. 'Not one of them asks for a calculator app.'
'You have ten of those on your page.'
'Ten. All from tutorials.' He crossed them out one by one. 'So what would they want to see? Something with real, messy data. Something that's actually running online.'
He wrote two lines: a dashboard of mandi onion prices from public records, cleaned and charted; and a bus-pass renewal tracker for his college, deployed with a live link. Two projects instead of ten.
Sangeeta read it over his shoulder. 'Onion prices? Our uncle will use that.'

qa.q: Which phrases did Ojas copy into his notebook?
How did Ojas feel crossing out the tutorial apps, and why?
qa.a: He likely felt some disappointment mixed with relief, seeing that none of the firms wanted calculator apps, which gave him a clearer target.

qa.q: What else could Ojas do to check the two projects hit the target?
qa.a: Show the plan to someone working at a similar firm or to the placement officer and ask whether these projects would catch their eye.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta see the onion price project?
qa.a: Sangeeta sees it as useful for their uncle, so the project feels real to the family and not only to recruiters.

grounding: Shows a student reading target job postings and choosing two projects that show data work and deployment instead of ten tutorial copies.

In her shared flat in Rotterdam, Dalia printed four job ads from the companies she most wanted, energy and shipping firms, and spread them on the kitchen table. Noa, her flatmate, came in with groceries and found her circling words in red.
'Everyone wants the same thing,' Dalia said. 'Look. Working with large data sets. Putting models into production. Not one says "has built a quiz app".'
'You have, like, nine quiz apps.'
'Nine, plus two weather ones.' She laughed, then went quiet. 'So I stop adding small ones. What would I need to show them?'
She wrote it out: one project that takes a big public data set, the port's ship arrival times, and cleans it properly; and one that turns it into a small forecasting tool that actually runs online.
Noa read the list. 'Two projects. That's scarier than eleven.'
'But they're the right two.'

qa.q: Which public data set did Dalia plan to use?
What was Dalia feeling when she laughed and then went quiet?
qa.a: She was probably amused at first, then uneasy, seeing that all her small apps did not match what the firms wanted.

qa.q: Which step would you add to Dalia's plan?
qa.a: Set a date for each of the two projects and ask someone in the industry for feedback on the first before starting the second.

qa.q: How does the new plan look to Noa?
qa.a: Noa finds two projects scarier than eleven, since fewer, bigger pieces feel riskier to someone watching from outside.

grounding: Shows a student working backward from what target firms ask for and choosing two projects on data handling and deployment instead of many small clones.
